observations.proposition: U.S. data centers are estimated to consume 521-843 TWh in 2030, corresponding to 9.5%-15.3% of total U.S. electricity use; the report reference case is 649 TWh / 11.8%.
EIA states electricity use by data centers is driving U.S. electricity demand growth and expects particularly fast near-term load growth in ERCOT and PJM.

At the end of 2024, roughly 10,300 projects were actively seeking U.S. transmission interconnection, representing about 1,400 GW of generation and 890 GW of storage; built projects from 2018-2024 had median interconnection-request-to-COD durations above four years in regions with data.

FERC Order No. 2023 reforms generator interconnection around cluster studies, readiness requirements, study deadlines, penalties, and affected-system procedures to address queue backlogs and improve processing.

DOE reports 2019 U.S. demand for new transformers above 60 MVA at about 750 units, with over 80% imported, and cites expected domestic demand rising to about 900 units annually by 2027; transmission expansion is identified as a primary demand driver.

DOE webinar material reports distribution-transformer lead times increasing from roughly 3-6 months in 2019 to 1-2 years or longer in 2024, with large transformers for substations and generators reaching roughly 3-4 years.

LBNL research finds data-center workload water use varies dramatically and is strongly affected by server efficiency, grid water factors, utilization, cooling system type, infrastructure efficiency, and climate zone.

NERC states new data centers for AI and the digital economy account for most projected North American electricity-demand growth over the next decade and present significant forecasting and planning challenges; Texas, PJM, and WECC report steep demand increases.

PJM reports unprecedented demand growth driven primarily by data centers; its 2025 planning forecast projected summer peak usage increasing by about 70 GW to 220 GW over 15 years, while later large-load evaluation indicated data-center growth up to roughly 30 GW between 2025 and 2030.
